frozen_original.title: DOGE Closed Social Security Offices, Left Disabled Facing 135-Mile Trips
frozen_original.synopsis: By February 2025, DOGE began closing at least 10 Social Security field offices, including the White Plains, NY hearing office serving seven counties with 2,000 pending cases. Closure would force elderly and disabled beneficiaries to travel up to 135 miles to the next office, potentially into another state. SSA staffing was already at a 50-year low when DOGE arrived, and ProPublica reported many closures targeted low-income, disabled, and orphaned recipients with no internet access.

primary.title: SSA Says White Plains Hearing-Office Closure Decision Dates to December 2024
primary.description_short: SSA said no local field offices had been permanently closed since Jan. 1, 2025, and dated the White Plains hearing-office decision to December 2024.
primary.description_medium: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration said it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office since Jan. 1. SSA distinguished those sites from one permanent hearing-office closure in White Plains, New York, and said most lease-termination sites were small hearing rooms without assigned employees. In October, SSA said the White Plains decision was made in December 2024 by the previous administration.
primary.description_long: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration issued a correction about reports that it was permanently closing local field offices. SSA said that since January 1 it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office. It distinguished those offices from one hearing office in White Plains, New York, whose permanent closure it had announced. The agency also said most sites it had sent to the General Services Administration for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms with no assigned employees. In an October 31 release, SSA said the White Plains hearing-office closure had been chosen in December 2024 by the previous administration. The release described a West Nyack hearing space intended to add in-person options for Hudson Valley claimants. This card records SSA’s clarification and the disclosed timeline. It does not claim that DOGE closed ten field offices in February. SSA’s releases do not substantiate the original item’s 135-mile travel figure, seven-county service count, 2,000-case backlog, or specific travel impacts on disabled and elderly beneficiaries; those claims are omitted.

frozen_original.title: Trump Administration Compiles Dossiers on Journalists and Political Opponents
frozen_original.synopsis: Reports emerged in mid-March 2025 that the Trump White House had directed intelligence and law enforcement agencies to compile dossiers on prominent journalists, Democratic politicians, and civil society leaders critical of the administration. The dossiers reportedly included surveillance records, financial information, personal communications, and compiled reporting on family members. The practice echoed the Nixon-era COINTELPRO programs and the FBI's files on political opponents. Press freedom organizations condemned the surveillance as an attempt to intimidate the free press and chill political opposition. Several Congress members demanded classified briefings on the scope of the surveillance program.

primary.title: State Department Official Requested Records About Journalists and Trump Critics
primary.description_short: A State Department official sought internal records involving journalists and Trump critics.
primary.description_medium: MIT Technology Review reported that a March 11, 2025 document from Trump appointee Darren Beattie requested State Department staff emails and other records involving journalists, researchers, organizations focused on foreign disinformation, and Trump critics. The request concerned records from the R/FIMI Hub. The reporting does not establish that intelligence agencies compiled the surveillance, financial, communications, or family dossiers alleged in the original entry.
primary.description_long: MIT Technology Review reported that a document dated March 11, 2025, and distributed in person to State Department employees in early March sought emails and other records from staff of the Counter Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference Hub (R/FIMI). The requested material concerned people and organizations that tracked or wrote about foreign disinformation, as well as critics of President Donald Trump and his allies; the report named journalists and former officials among those referenced. Trump appointee Darren Beattie framed the request as a transparency initiative, according to the article. This is a documented internal records request by a State Department official. It does not establish that a White House-wide directive reached intelligence or law-enforcement agencies, or that dossiers containing surveillance records, financial information, private communications, and family material were actually compiled. The report also does not document a resulting investigation or publication of those records. This entry is narrowed to the reported request and keeps its scope and effects distinct from the unsupported claims in the frozen version.

frozen_original.title: Trump Installs FISA Court Loyalists Who Approve Surveillance of Political Opponents
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, following the removal of FISA Court judges who had resisted certain surveillance requests, the Trump administration installed new FISA Court judges — designated from among district judges known to be aligned with the administration's expansive view of executive surveillance power — who subsequently approved surveillance applications that prior judges had declined. Reports emerged that the new FISA Court composition had authorized monitoring of communications of individuals associated with political opposition figures, journalists, and civil society groups. Intelligence community veterans warned the weaponization of FISA Court composition to enable surveillance of political opponents represented the most dangerous use of intelligence surveillance tools against American civil liberties since COINTELPRO. Congressional oversight committees were denied access to relevant FISA applications under an expansive assertion of executive privilege.

blockers: The original core claim says President Trump removed FISC judges and installed loyalists. The official court description states that FISC judges are federal district judges designated by the Chief Justice; the supplied packet contains no evidence of a Trump removal or installation in March 2025.

The claims that replacement judges approved surveillance applications previously rejected, targeted political opponents, journalists, or civil-society groups, and that Congress was denied records under executive privilege have no supporting source evidence in the supplied packet or search results.

The two accessed official court pages establish the court’s designation process and roster, but do not support a narrower Trump-directed event. Exclusion is proposed because the event’s central mechanism and alleged actions remain unsupported.
primary.exact_blocker: No source identifies a March 2025 Trump action changing FISC membership or authorizing the specific surveillance described. Official FISC materials say its members are designated by the Chief Justice and list designation dates; no supplied or retrieved source substantiates the asserted removal, loyalist replacements, targeting, or executive-privilege denial.
